name: Kobon
confidence_why: Davies 1980 says stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, but Davies 1981 says vowel strength conditions its position, and the reanalyses of his data split: Kenstowicz 1997 argues for sonority-driven stress within the last two syllables while Rasin 2018 finds only a near-tie between that and a penultimate rule with weight exceptions, so Shih and de Lacy 2019 list Kobon among the languages whose stress placement is disputed.
catalog_quote: The phonological word is a rhythm unit having one major stress placement, the physical manifestation of stress being relatively greater intensity often accompanied by relatively higher pitch. In general the boundaries of phonological and grammatical words coincide.

tone_statements.citation: Davies, H.J. (1980). Kobon Phonology. Pacific Linguistics Series B, No 68.
tone_statements.quote: as either level or gliding tone may occur, and as new phonemes do not need to be set up … The phonological word … is a rhythm unit having one major stress placement, a composite of higher pitch and intensity. … it appears that stress is not phonemic. In phonological words of more than one syllable stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable. … The phonological sentence … is the unit of intonation placement in the phonological hierarchy. It is bounded by pause, and is characterised by an undulating intonation contour and a down-glide on the final syllable.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: No tonemes: pitch figures only in the one non-phonemic word stress (normally penultimate) and in sentence intonation (final down-glide); level or gliding pitch on /ai au/ is free; remarks tentative.

audit.recode_to: segmental (vowel-quality/sonority-conditioned stress within a final two-syllable window, penult on ties/default; hierarchy a/au/ai > o/e/u/i > ə/ɨ per Davies 1981:226; verbs: suffix-determined, 3sg present final per Davies 1980:59) — the class the catalog already uses for Ama. If a positional class must be kept, 'fixed-dominant' penult (Davies 1980:58 'normally'; Davies 1981:226 'such cases are very few' for trisyllables) with a quality caution, never 'fixed-strict'. 'conflict' is defensible too (Davies 1980 vs 1981; Rasin 2018 tie).

sources.citation: Shih, Shu-hao & Paul de Lacy. 2019. Evidence for sonority-driven stress. Catalan Journal of Linguistics 18: 9-40 (open access, DOI 10.5565/rev/catjl.256).
sources.quote: Table 2 lists three Kobon 'versions': (a) Davies (1981) a au ai > o e u i > ə ɨ; (b) Kenstowicz (1997) a > e o > i u > ə > ɨ; (c) Davies (1980) 'Penultimate stress'; text: 'Disagreements about stress assignment were found in ... Kobon. Even more significantly, Raisin (2017) argues that the data for Kobon presented in the primary sources does not support the generalizations made about sonority-driven stress by Kenstowicz (1997) and others.' No instrumental data for Kobon.
sources.note: Most recent survey; documents that the Kobon descriptions (Davies 1980 vs 1981 vs Kenstowicz) disagree and that no instrumental study exists — supports a hedged/conflict coding rather than fixed-strict.
